title: Superconducting circuits host two-level systems with lifetimes exceeding one second
authors: Mathieu Féchant, Phillip Lenhard, Nicolas Gosling, Ritika Dhundhwal, Denis Bénâtre, Wolfgang Wernsdorfer, Thomas Reisinger, Ioan M. Pop
abstract: Understanding the microscopic environment of superconducting qubits is a central challenge for quantum technologies. Parasitic two-level systems (TLSs) of various microscopic origins are ubiquitous and limit qubit performance through decoherence, frequency drifts, and leakage. Recently, long-lived TLSs with lifetimes exceeding those of state-of-the-art qubits have been shown to induce correlated qubit dynamics, with direct implications for quantum error correction. Here, we perform wide-band quantum-jump correlation spectroscopy on flux-tunable transmon qubits and identify microscopic degrees of freedom that outlive the qubit by orders of magnitude. Pump-probe measurements at varying detunings from these objects reveal intrinsic lifetimes exceeding one second. Their weak coupling to the qubit, in the kilohertz range, is consistent with positional defects described by the standard tunneling model, without excluding other microscopic origins such as magnetic spin impurities or trapped quasiparticles. More broadly, these results establish superconducting qubits as a sensitive probe of exceptionally long-lived microscopic degrees of freedom and open a route toward their controlled access and functionalization.
summary: This paper investigates the microscopic environment of superconducting qubits by measuring parasitic Two-Level Systems (TLSs). Using advanced quantum-jump and pump-probe techniques, the researchers identified TLSs with remarkably long lifetimes, exceeding one second. This work not only characterizes these limiting defects but also establishes superconducting qubits as a powerful tool for probing fundamental, long-lived quantum noise sources.
main_problem: The central challenge in superconducting qubits is understanding the parasitic Two-Level Systems (TLSs) that limit performance through decoherence and frequency drifts.
main_result: The authors identified microscopic TLSs with intrinsic lifetimes exceeding one second, establishing superconducting qubits as a sensitive probe for these long-lived environmental degrees of freedom.
method: The study employed wide-band quantum-jump correlation spectroscopy and pump-probe measurements at varying detunings to characterize the TLS dynamics.
model_or_system: The platform is flux-tunable transmon qubits fabricated on superconducting circuits. The environment is modeled by coupling the qubit to TLSs, whose interaction is analyzed using quantum jump theory and Solomon equations.
key_observables: Intrinsic TLS relaxation time (T_TLS) measured in the seconds range, qubit population dynamics after quantum jumps, and TLS spectral features.
important_parameters: TLS coupling strength (in the kHz range), detuning ($\delta$), and the qubit's coherence time ($T_1$).
main_assumptions: The weak coupling to the TLSs is consistent with positional defects described by the standard tunneling model, though other origins are not excluded.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate quantum jump spectroscopy results, pump-probe sequences showing population evolution, and plots detailing the measured intrinsic TLS lifetimes as a function of detuning.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the problem of TLS-induced decoherence, then detailing the quantum-jump and pump-probe measurement techniques, culminating in the measurement and characterization of ultra-long-lived TLSs.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the environmental coupling mechanisms crucial for building fault-tolerant quantum computers, providing quantitative measurements of decoherence sources.
